subject: RE: [distance-sampling] CTDS - impact of deviation from predefined snapshot moment

messages.subject: RE: [distance-sampling] CTDS - impact of deviation from predefined snapshot moment
parts:
Olly, I think bias would vary substantially from one application to another.  It will be a strong function of how animals move for example.  But it seems to me that you might be asking the wrong question.  I can’t see the variation in gaps between images within a burst being an issue, but what is an issue is separation between one burst and the next.  If your snapshot moments were entirely independent of what animals are doing, the gap between snapshot moments could be whatever you choose.  If you choose a long gap, there would be fewer images to store and analyse, but also fewer detections, so it would be a compromise which affects precision and cost but not bias.  However, if you only take images when an animal is present, then the snapshot separation needs to be short, so that animals cannot pass in front of the camera without being recorded.  For a given animal pass, you can define the first snapshot moment to be the moment the camera first triggers.  Then you would want it to trigger again 2s later – or whatever time separation you have selected.  I don’t see why you would select burst mode, as you would then want the next burst starting immediately.  So why not have the camera in single-image mode, and set so that it triggers every 2s (say) until the animal has passed out of the detection area?  If your animals are slow-moving and detectable at large distances, you could have much longer than 2s between snapshot moments.

 

I’m copying this to Eric Howe, who may have comments to add.

 

Steve

From: distance...@googlegroups.com [mailto:distance...@googlegroups.com] On Behalf Of Olly Griffin
Sent: 04 December 2020 09:53
To: distance-sampling <distance...@googlegroups.com>
Subject: [distance-sampling] CTDS - impact of deviation from predefined snapshot moment

 

Hi list, 

 

In Howe et al. 2017, the authors discuss selection of pre-defined snapshot moments, typically in 2 second increments past the minute (e.g. 08:03:00, 08:03:02, 08:03:04, ... 08:03:58 etc). This is done to avoid bias in animal detection distances, which could occur due to the conical shape of the field of view of a camera trap. To quote:

"Observed distances upon first detection are expected to be positively biased because animals entering the detection zone through the arc of the sector would contribute a disproportionate number of observations at far distances. Bias would be slight if the time between snapshot moments (t) was small enough to ensure that the animals did not move far relative to the range of the sensor between snapshots, as then the observations would be representative of animals’ continuous paths past the CTs. However, we prefer to avoid the potential for bias by assuming that the snapshot moments are selected independently of animal locations, and predetermining them as specific times of day to ensure that the assumption is met."

 

This effect is illustrated in Eric's PhD thesis in more detail (see Figure 3.1): Howe, E. J. (2019). Estimating abundance of African great apes. University of St Andrews. Available from http://hdl.handle.net/10023/18859.

In Cappelle et al. 2019, the authors state they used a t  of 2 seconds, but from the start of each captured video, rather than predetermined based on time of day:

"We recorded observation distances between cameras and the midpoints of each filmed chimpanzee at 2‐s intervals (i.e., at 0, 2, 4, …, 58 s after the start of the video),  independent of whether single individuals or groups were seen."

 

Despite this, this CTDS survey produced accurate results compared to other survey methods and to the known size of chimpanzee groups. Talking with Noémie, she thought that with a t of 2s, the difference between using snapshots defined from time vs from video start would be small.

 

This leads to my main question, which is: is there any estimate available on the size of this potential bias?

I'll explain the context of my question in relation to our planned survey, in case this has a bearing on the answer...

We plan to use photo captures, rather than video, due to data management constraints - it's a large survey, in areas with poor internet connectivity, with a limited number of technical staff to process video. Photos will likely generated a smaller dataset (in terms of GB/TB), and be quicker to classify (AI classification for video is not yet widely available, but can be run locally for images), especially for non-technical staff (a folder based system with photos like the Sanderson workflow can be used by anyone able to use a computer), and measuring distances from a subset of photos will be quicker and simpler than finding specific frames within a video file and measuring at those points.

We had assumed that the burst mode on the cameras available would be something like Photo Mode 3 in this image, which I've shared on this group before: https://imgur.com/a/8u63uIq (apologies, images don't seem to paste in-line in this group).

 

However, following a pilot, it looks like it is closer to Photo Mode 2 in that image, as the delay between images within a burst vary between ~0.3 and ~0.6s, with the first 3 images of 5 being within the first second, and the following 2 of 5 taken around 0.6 second after that (i.e. photos captured at about :00.300, :00.600, :00.900, :01.500, and :02.100). A single image can be taken with burst mode off, with an interval of 0.6 seconds (i.e. at :00.600. :01.200, :01.800, :02.400, :03.000 etc), which would also reduce empty images compared to a 5-burst set up.

 

In addition, milliseconds are not recorded to the metadata by the camera trap firmware, making it difficult (or impossible) to know which image is closer to a snapshot, one taken 10ms before the snapshot, or 400 ms after the snapshot (as they are rounded to the second, or just have the milliseconds dropped, I'm not sure which).

 

We can still programmatically select images close/closest to the snapshot moment, which was the original intention, but the average difference between when the selected image was taken and the snapshot moment will be larger than anticipated, and have at least an element of structure (i.e. non-random, as it will be related to the initial trigger to a degree (but not always X seconds after the initial trigger, as the interval  (0.6) is not a integer or factor of t. This means detections will not necessarily be equally spaced by exactly 2 seconds, but may be 2 seconds +/- up to ~0.4s deviation.


So to reiterate my main question, and add some related ones:

  1. Is there any estimate available on the size of this potential bias (snap shot moments not fully independent of initial capture)? 
  2. Is it likely to be small enough (with t = 2s) that it can be tolerated for the sake of practicality?
    • I assume the bias in our context would be smaller than in Cappelle et al. 2019 as, whilst not perfectly aligned with independent snapshot moments, the degree to which the detection distance is based on the moment of initial capture is reduced.
  1. What might be the impact of using snapshot moments that are not equally spaced?
    • For example, selecting images closest to independent snapshot moments, but which end up being from e.g. :00.300, :01.800, :04.200 etc rather than on each second exactly.
  1. Is there anything that could be done within the context above to reduce the potential bias as much as possible?
    • I assume decreasing t to 1s would help, but using images, the detections would still not be selected from a continuous range of times, but come from a set of quantized available images, as determined by the interval and trigger speed.

Thanks as always for your invaluable advice!

Cheers,

 

Olly
